artworks.title: Heracles Finding the Infant Telephus Suckled by a Deer
artworks.description: This Roman fresco from Herculaneum, now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, renders the foundational image of the Telephus legend: the hero Heracles discovering the son he fathered on the Tegean priestess Auge. Exposed as an infant on Mount Parthenius, the babe was suckled by a doe that had just cast its fawn — the marvel that, by Apollodorus' etymology, gave the child his name (Bibliotheca 2.7.4). The painting personifies the Mysian landscape as a seated woman of Arcadia, with the eagle of Heracles, a lion, and the nursing deer gathered around the muscular figure of the hero, who gazes at the child he does not yet know.

artworks.title: Telephus Seated on the Altar with Bandaged Thigh
artworks.description: On this Athenian red-figure pelike in the British Museum (E 382), Telephus appears as the wounded suppliant — the iconographic moment popularised by Euripides' lost tragedy. King of Mysia, Telephus had been wounded in the thigh by Achilles' Pelian spear when the Greek fleet mistakenly landed in his realm; an oracle of Apollo declared the wound could be healed only by the weapon that made it (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.17–20). The vase shows him seated on an altar, his injured leg conspicuously bound, in the posture of the ragged stranger who has come to the Greek camp to beg the cure and, in exchange, to guide the army to Troy.

artworks.title: Telephus Threatening the Infant Orestes (Telephus Frieze, Panel 42)
artworks.description: Part of the inner Telephus frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, now in the Antikensammlung of Berlin, this marble relief depicts the hostage scene preserved in Hyginus (Fabulae 101): unable to obtain healing, Telephus seizes the infant Orestes from the altar and threatens to kill him unless the Achaeans relieve his wound. The Pergamene kings claimed descent from Telephus, and the long frieze narrates his entire saga — birth, exposure, kingship of Mysia, the wound and its cure — in a continuous pictorial cycle that is the most ambitious ancient artwork devoted to the hero. Here the desperate king and the imperilled child are caught at the altar's edge in high dramatic tension.

artworks.title: Achilles Healing Telephus with the Rust of His Spear
artworks.description: This marble bas-relief, found in the House of the Relief of Telephus at Herculaneum and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples (inv. 6591), illustrates the climax of the legend and gives the house its name. Following Apollo's oracle that the wounder must become the healer, Achilles scrapes the rust from the very Pelian spear that pierced Telephus' thigh and applies it to the wound (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.20; Ovid, Metamorphoses 12–13). The composition shows the seated, suffering king and the figures attending the cure, after which a healed Telephus pilots the Greek fleet to Troy — the indispensable role that bound his fate to the war.
